maxwell.title: Maxwell's equations, complete
maxwell.caption: The same grid as the intro course, with the two empty cells filled. A changing B drives circulating E (Faraday); a changing E acts like a current and drives circulating B (displacement current). The rows now talk to each other — that coupling is what makes waves. Grey boxes are from Introduction to EMF.

columns.label: How does the field spread out?  (divergence · flux)
How does the field circulate?  (curl · circulation)

nodes.name: Faraday's law (integral)
nodes.summary: A changing magnetic flux through a loop drives an EMF around it — a circulating electric field. The cell of the static grid that read ∮E·dl = 0 now has a right-hand side.

nodes.name: ∇×E = −∂B/∂t
nodes.summary: Faraday's law at a point, via Stokes' theorem. The electric field is no longer conservative when B varies in time, so a scalar potential alone no longer describes it.

nodes.name: Motional and transformer EMF
nodes.summary: Two ways to change flux: move the conductor through a field (motional EMF, from the Lorentz force) or change the field through a fixed loop (transformer EMF). Both are Faraday's law.

nodes.name: Displacement current
nodes.summary: A changing electric field acts like a current density ∂D/∂t. Maxwell added it so that Ampère's law stays consistent with charge conservation — and in doing so predicted electromagnetic waves.

nodes.name: Continuity equation
nodes.summary: Charge is conserved: current flowing out of a region reduces the charge inside it. Taking the divergence of Ampère's static law contradicts this unless displacement current is added.

nodes.name: Ampère–Maxwell law (integral)
nodes.summary: Ampère's law with displacement current: the circulation of H counts conduction current plus the rate of change of electric flux through the loop.

nodes.name: ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t
nodes.summary: The Ampère–Maxwell law at a point. Together with Faraday's law it couples E and B: each one's change drives the other's circulation.

nodes.name: Maxwell's equations, complete
nodes.summary: All four laws with their time-dependent terms, in integral and differential form, plus the constitutive relations D = εE, B = μH, J = σE. Everything in this course follows from these.

nodes.name: Time-varying potentials V and A
nodes.summary: With B = ∇×A, Faraday's law gives E = −∇V − ∂A/∂t. Choosing the Lorenz gauge turns Maxwell's equations into wave equations for V and A with sources ρ and J.

nodes.name: The wave equation
nodes.summary: Take the curl of Faraday's law, substitute the Ampère–Maxwell law, and in a source-free region each field satisfies a wave equation with speed 1/√(με). In vacuum that speed is c.

nodes.name: Phasors and time-harmonic fields
nodes.summary: For sinusoidal steady state, replace ∂/∂t with jω and work with complex amplitudes. Maxwell's equations become algebraic in time; the wave equation becomes the Helmholtz equation.

nodes.name: Uniform plane waves in lossless media
nodes.summary: The simplest solution: E and H perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, in phase, with E/H fixed by the medium. Wavelength, phase velocity and wavenumber follow.

nodes.name: Intrinsic impedance η
nodes.summary: The ratio of E to H in a plane wave, set by the medium: √(μ/ε), about 377 Ω in free space. It plays the role for waves that characteristic impedance plays for transmission lines.

nodes.name: Wave polarization
nodes.summary: The path traced by the tip of E as the wave passes: linear, circular or elliptical, depending on the relative amplitude and phase of two perpendicular components.

nodes.name: Waves in lossy media
nodes.summary: With conductivity, the wavenumber becomes complex: the wave attenuates as it travels and E and H fall out of phase. The loss tangent σ/ωε says whether a material acts like a dielectric or a conductor at a given frequency.

nodes.name: Good conductors and skin depth
nodes.summary: In a good conductor the wave dies out within a skin depth δ = 1/α, which shrinks with frequency. High-frequency current flows only in a thin surface layer — why RF conductors are plated and why shielding works.

nodes.name: Poynting vector and power flow
nodes.summary: E × H is power per unit area carried by the field. Its divergence accounts for the energy stored in E and B and the power dissipated as heat — conservation of energy for fields.

nodes.name: Normal incidence on a boundary
nodes.summary: A plane wave hitting an interface splits into reflected and transmitted waves. The boundary conditions on tangential E and H fix the reflection and transmission coefficients in terms of the two impedances.

nodes.name: Standing waves
nodes.summary: Incident and reflected waves interfere into a pattern that does not travel: nodes and antinodes fixed in space. The standing-wave ratio measures how much is reflected.

nodes.name: Oblique incidence; Snell's law
nodes.summary: At an angle, the wave's parallel and perpendicular polarizations reflect differently. Matching phase along the boundary gives the law of reflection and Snell's law.

nodes.name: Brewster angle
nodes.summary: At one angle of incidence the parallel-polarized reflection vanishes entirely. Reflected light at that angle is fully polarized — the principle behind polarizing sunglasses.

nodes.name: Total internal reflection
nodes.summary: Going from a denser to a lighter medium past the critical angle, nothing is transmitted — the field beyond the boundary is evanescent. Optical fibers run on this.

nodes.name: Distributed line parameters R, L, G, C
nodes.summary: A transmission line is capacitance and inductance per unit length (plus loss). The C and L you computed for coax and parallel plates in the intro course are exactly these.

nodes.name: Telegrapher's equations
nodes.summary: Kirchhoff's laws applied to a short length of line give coupled equations for V and I along it. They are the wave equation again, for voltage and current instead of E and H.
nodes.equation: \frac{\partial V}{\partial z} = -L'\frac{\partial I}{\partial t},\qquad \frac{\partial I}{\partial z} = -C'\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}

nodes.name: Characteristic impedance Z₀
nodes.summary: The ratio of voltage to current for a wave traveling one way on the line, fixed by geometry and material. The transmission-line twin of intrinsic impedance.

nodes.name: Reflection coefficient at a load
nodes.summary: A load that does not equal Z₀ reflects part of the wave. Same formula as normal incidence on a boundary, with impedances instead of η.

nodes.name: Standing-wave ratio on a line
nodes.summary: The voltage standing-wave pattern on a mismatched line; VSWR is what you read on an instrument to judge a match.

nodes.name: Input impedance of a line
nodes.summary: Looking into a length of line terminated in Z_L you see a different impedance, periodic in quarter wavelengths. Shorted and open stubs become inductors and capacitors; the quarter-wave transformer follows.

nodes.name: The Smith chart
nodes.summary: A graphical map of the reflection coefficient on which impedances, admittances and line lengths can be read off. Still the standard way to think about matching.

nodes.name: Transients and bounce diagrams
nodes.summary: A step launched onto a line bounces between source and load; the bounce diagram tracks each reflection. This is the time-domain picture behind signal-integrity problems on circuit boards.

nodes.name: Rectangular waveguide modes
nodes.summary: Confine a wave between conducting walls and only certain field patterns (TE and TM modes) satisfy the boundary conditions. Each has a cutoff frequency below which it will not propagate.

nodes.name: The Hertzian dipole
nodes.summary: A short current element with time-varying current radiates. Solving for its retarded vector potential gives near fields that look like the static dipole and far fields that are outgoing waves.

nodes.name: Radiation pattern, directivity, gain
nodes.summary: How radiated power varies with direction, and the single numbers that summarize it. Radiation resistance connects the antenna back to circuit theory.

nodes.name: Optics and photonics
nodes.summary: Reflection, refraction, polarization and total internal reflection at optical frequencies are the same physics with ε set by the material at ~10¹⁴ Hz. Fiber, thin films and lasers start here.

nodes.name: RF and microwave design
nodes.summary: Matching networks, filters, amplifiers and antennas as engineered components. Everything on the Smith chart and in the antenna unit is the entry ticket.

nodes.name: Signal integrity and high-speed digital
nodes.summary: Fast edges on circuit-board traces are transmission-line transients. Reflections, crosstalk and termination are the bounce diagram applied to real boards.

nodes.name: Software-defined radio
nodes.summary: Phasors and time-harmonic fields are the physics; DSP is what you do with the sampled result. SDR is where this course meets signals and code.
